name: Karl Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Karl, 43, and I lead difficult wiring and repair jobs in homes and businesses. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the strongest electricians in our crew, but my pay is low. My partner cooks part-time in a community kitchen; we have children aged twelve and sixteen, a mortgage and twenty-four days of expenses saved. There are few other electrical employers nearby, and I use AI daily for checked notes and parts comparisons without handing over the safety decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the small useful parts are still useful. I use AI daily to sort my checked notes and compare parts descriptions, not to decide an installation is safe. I'd rather show an apprentice why a test matters than argue that a computer will either save or ruin everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be anxious about paid hours. I'm a lead electrician and one of the strongest people in our crew, but the wage is low and we need some extra calls for school and replacement costs. We have twenty-four days of expenses saved, and the owner hasn't confirmed next month's extras, so the mortgage budget isn't as solid as my job title sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading repairs and checking the crew's finished work. This week I'd ask the owner which extra calls were genuinely paid and confirmed, then budget from those rather than a busy-looking diary. In the first year I'd keep a record of actual wages and household bills with my partner each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though not about whether I can do tomorrow's repair. I can explain a difficult circuit in simple words. I can't explain a missing wage into the bank account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What qualifications and responsibility are behind that title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm 43. I lead the awkward home and business repairs and decide when the crew needs another check before proceeding. My reputation is strong, but there are few other electrical firms nearby bidding to pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who shares the household costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner cooks part-time in a community kitchen, and our children are twelve and sixteen. We have a mortgage, and the children still need things whether extra repair calls arrive or not. I don't mind using a clever tool; I mind a useful worker being told that a full toolbox should be enough security.

say: I'd keep **useful small tools** without turning them into a story that promises everything or nothing.
I'd explain **tests to apprentices** rather than let a tidy AI draft replace understanding.
think: My **lead responsibility** and strong skill still come with low pay and reliance on extra calls.
With **twenty-four days saved**, unconfirmed extra work leaves mortgage and school costs uncertain despite a senior title.
do: Keep **leading repairs** and checking finished crew work through the first year.
Confirm **paid extra calls** this week and count only agreed work in the household budget.
Review **actual wages** and bills with my partner monthly rather than rely on the diary.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours, with confidence in technical work that does not translate into financial security.
S0.quote: I can't explain a missing wage into the bank account.
fieldNote: His **high standing** appears in difficult repairs, crew checks, a technical diploma and master electrician's licence, without a matching comfortable wage.
His **daily AI use** is routine checked assistance, while the baseline worry concerns unconfirmed extra earnings and a thin family reserve.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and count only confirmed paid extra calls in the household budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's test the new tools and let the workers see the errors, not just the sales figures. I'd offer a small paid trial of AI-prepared job checklists. I'd want the apprentice to know who checks a mistake, rather than be the cheapest person left to explain it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part of my lead role could get much quicker, but I worry the owner would keep the responsibility and reduce the paid time for it. My own hours or extras could shrink while the crew still needed hands on the wiring. Enjoying a new tool doesn't mean I can afford that change at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a three-job AI checklist trial this month on completed work, during paid hours with normal weekly wage and hours unchanged. I'd compare every proposed check with the actual job and stop if important steps were missing or unexplained. In the first year I'd take anonymised errors to the staff's joint safety discussion and sign a request for paid learning and a named person responsible for checking software drafts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage, and keen to find out what the tool really does. I don't need to be the person who guessed correctly in an argument. I want the apprentice safe and the work paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you refuse in that trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unpaid evening work, or a real installation relying on a draft we hadn't checked. I'd ask the employer to schedule paid time and keep current safety checks in place. If that wasn't agreed, the trial wouldn't start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the errors to a joint discussion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the next worker should not have to discover the same omission alone. We'd remove customer details and talk about the check, not blame an apprentice for a software mistake. I'd sign the group's request, while recognising a request wasn't yet an employer agreement.

say: I'd share **tool errors** with workers rather than show only sales figures.
I'd name who **checks drafts** so an apprentice isn't left carrying responsibility for a mistake.
think: Quicker **lead-role paperwork** could leave the same responsibility with fewer paid hours.
My **household budget** cannot ignore lost extras simply because I enjoy testing the technology.
do: Trial **AI checklists** on three completed jobs only in paid time with normal weekly wage and hours unchanged.
Compare **every check** with actual work and stop if important omissions cannot be explained.
Share **anonymised errors** at a joint safety discussion and sign a request for paid learning and named draft checkers.
feel: **Anxious** about income and interested in evidence, with apprentice safety and paid time as practical limits.
S1.quote: I want the apprentice safe and the work paid for.
fieldNote: His **new learning** is a bounded AI checklist trial, distinct from routine daily notes and supported by completed-job evidence and paid time.
The **group action** includes a signed request and shared error discussion, without inventing either employer agreement or apprentice responsibility for unchecked software.

steps.text: Trial AI checklists on three completed jobs in paid time with unchanged weekly wage and hours
Sign joint request for paid learning and named checkers after sharing anonymised checklist errors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 reaches planning first, then capable robots around 2031 reach the physical jobs. I'd tell my family that being quick with software doesn't put us outside that picture. I'd want people to ask what work and income actually remain instead of treating a licence as a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect capable robots to remove a large share of the ordinary installation hours that fund our wages. Difficult repairs might remain for a time, but I wouldn't count on enough to replace everything the household needs. My partner's cooking is physical too, so I can't call that wage a permanent fallback when we have only twenty-four days saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop buying new games now and put the usual 20 monthly into the reserve only when actual wages covered essentials. I'd ask the union adviser about any public or lender support, checking eligibility and full costs rather than assume help existed. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep real paid repairs and join a staff request for confirmed hours and paid learning while work changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a large loss of income when robots follow, even though I can still organise the next steps. I wake up imagining the mortgage amount and a payslip that doesn't meet it. I'd rather admit the fear than let my children think being good at work means never needing help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count support as income before applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask what we might qualify for and use the existing budget until anything was actually approved or agreed. A lender option could also have fees or later costs, which I'd want explained. My partner would see the terms before either of us agreed to change the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why save only 20 if the risk is so large?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's the spending I can name and stop without guessing at money we don't have. If essentials used the money, the deposit would wait rather than come from borrowing. I'd rather pause a 20 monthly deposit than borrow money to pretend the reserve was growing.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031 reaching the physical jobs.
I'd ask about **real work and income** rather than call software confidence or a licence permanent protection.
think: I expect a large **installation-hours loss** once robots arrive, without enough difficult repairs to replace all needed earnings.
My partner's **cooking wage** also faces the physical endpoint, and our twenty-four-day reserve provides little time.
do: Stop **new game purchases** now and save 20 monthly only while actual wages cover essentials.
Ask the **union adviser** about eligibility and full costs for real support, assuming no income until approval or agreement.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and join a request for confirmed hours and paid learning.
feel: **Alarmed** about expected later household losses, with interrupted sleep despite retaining a plan and willingness to seek help.
S2.quote: I'd rather pause a 20 monthly deposit than borrow money to pretend the reserve was growing.
fieldNote: He locates the **expected major loss** in the physical robot phase, while keeping actual paid repairs during the first post-2028 year.
The **support inquiry** preserves eligibility, approval and lender costs, and the new deposit has a named spending source subordinate to essential bills.

steps.text: Save 20 monthly from games only after actual wages cover essentials
Ask union adviser about support eligibility costs and required approvals before assuming income
Join staff request for confirmed paid hours and paid learning in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to work on the rules as well as our own tool skills. Thinking AI comes in 2031 and robots around 2034, so I'd want paid adult learning and income protection discussed before the losses. I'd still turn up and lead the work that exists, not wait for a campaign to pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 in 2031, with children about seventeen and twenty-one, and I don't know what help either would still need. My current thin reserve and uncertain extras still worry me. Longer warning gives us time to organise, but I can't put a policy I favour into the household income column.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join union colleagues this month in a campaign for paid adult learning and temporary income support after actual earnings loss, writing to a representative about the gap in our own budget. I'd continue the 20 monthly deposit only after essential bills were covered. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid repairs and check any actual training or support offer for eligibility, fees and effects on paid hours before accepting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more time to make the case in daylight instead of only doing sums at night. I don't imagine a letter changes the rules by itself. I'd rather join an effort to change them than tell every apprentice their only answer is to be faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the letter actually ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid practical learning that workers can use without missing their household income, and temporary support tied to real earnings lost. I'd describe my low pay and the time it takes to train someone safely. I'd ask for a response, not announce that the proposal had become a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop your own learning while campaigning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still test useful tools in agreed paid time with the checks the job required. The campaign isn't a substitute for work or competence. Individual effort and a usable shared arrangement can both matter.

say: I'd seek **paid learning** and support rules before actual losses rather than rely only on individual speed.
I'd keep **leading existing work** without treating a campaign as money already available.
think: At **48**, I'd still need wages and couldn't assume older children had no further support needs.
Our **thin reserve** and uncertain extras remain worrying, while a policy I support is not current household income.
do: Join the **union campaign** now and write to a representative seeking paid adult learning and temporary support after actual earnings loss.
Save **20 monthly** only after essential household bills are covered.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and check actual offers for eligibility, fees and effects on paid hours before acceptance.
feel: **Anxious** about present finances, with time for shared action rather than only private worry.
S3.quote: I can't put a policy I favour into the household income column.
fieldNote: His **political action** is a campaign and letter with a defined ask, distinct from claiming an entitlement or guaranteed payment.
He keeps **individual competence** and paid work alongside collective aims, checking real offers rather than assuming the campaign resolves affordability.

steps.text: Join union campaign; write a representative requesting paid learning and temporary support after actual earnings loss
Save 20 monthly only after essential household bills are covered
Keep paid repairs after 2031 and check offer eligibility fees and paid-hour effects

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to teach people properly and argue about who pays before the last minute. I'd want the children to look at different kinds of work rather than follow a headline. I'd still favour paid practical learning, not a requirement that everybody spends the family's evenings proving they're adaptable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when capable robots followed, so retirement isn't a safe assumption. Low pay, unconfirmed extra calls and twenty-four days saved still leave me anxious about an ordinary missed wage now. My partner's physical work isn't a permanent escape either; the longer warning just gives us more time to respond.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the campaign and the conditional 20 monthly deposit going now, stopping the deposit if essentials needed the money. I'd ask the school this year about free work visits chosen by the children rather than choose a career for them. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repair work, checking actual support or training terms before counting any help or taking on costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's money, with less hurry about the dates. I'd enjoy having years to teach an apprentice without acting as though next Tuesday is the end of useful work. I can be curious and frightened without either feeling cancelling the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the school visits be a new cost to the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask only about free visits that fitted the school arrangements and the children's interests. If extra travel or fees appeared, we'd check the budget and not promise a place automatically. I want choices explored, not another bill signed without thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a child who liked your trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the real work, including the patient checking and the days when the wage disappoints. I'd help the child ask about paid learning and actual jobs. My diploma and licence tell you what I learned, not what your whole working life must be.

say: I'd use **ten years** for proper paid teaching rather than demand unpaid family evenings as proof of adaptability.
I'd support **varied work visits** chosen by the children instead of steer their lives from a headline.
think: I can't assume **retirement** at 53 or when robots arrive around 56.
Our low pay and **thin reserve** still make missed wages worrying, while both physical jobs face later uncertainty.
do: Save **20 monthly** now only after essential household bills are covered, pausing the deposit if that money is needed.
Ask school about **free child-chosen visits**, making no automatic commitment to added travel or fees.
Continue **campaigning** now while keeping paid repairs after 2036, checking support or training terms before counting help or accepting costs.
feel: **Anxious** about current finances, with less urgency and continued curiosity about what can improve.
S4.quote: My diploma and licence tell you what I learned, not what your whole working life must be.
fieldNote: His **long warning** preserves present earnings worries without assuming retirement, cleared debt or physical work exempt from the robot endpoint.
His **children's visits** remain free, chosen and checked for extra costs, while campaign aims and saving targets stay separate from guaranteed income.

steps.text: Continue campaign for paid adult learning and support after actual earnings loss
Save 20 monthly only after actual wages cover essential bills
Keep paid repairs after 2036 and verify support or training terms before counting help

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could remove a large share of the physical work supporting both household wages. Paid learning, confirmed work hours and real income support after losses would help. I'd want workers involved in the rules, and every offer checked for what it actually pays and costs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a person who likes tools also wants the rules to be fair. I can test the cleverest tool in the room and still need the same wage protection as the apprentice. Curiosity isn't an agreement to carry the whole cost of change alone.

headlineQuote: I can test the cleverest tool in the room and still need the same wage protection as the apprentice.
portrait: Karl, **43**, is a highly skilled repair lead with a two-year technical diploma, master electrician's licence and low pay.
His **partner cooks part-time**, with two school-age children, a mortgage, twenty-four days saved and few nearby electrical employers.
He uses **AI daily**, testing new checklists only with paid time, unchanged wages and hours, completed-job comparisons and shared error checks.
His **campaign and saving plans** preserve actual-loss eligibility and essential bills, without treating political aims or a small deposit as replacement wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little preparation time before robots around 2031 could remove much of the physical work supporting both household incomes.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid learning** and confirmed hours would let workers maintain income while adapting.
Real **income support after losses**, with worker involvement and fully checked terms, would help beyond individual tool skills.
